sources.title: S. G. Agajanov, The States of the Oghuz, the Kimek and the Kipchak (1998), UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia IV/1
sources.note: Original scholarly chapter read through full-volume mirror, printed74-77. Political chronology, herding/housing, crafts and fragmentation. All mirrors of this volume treated as same work for attribution; no runtime source title/URL variant found in reuse scan. Later al-Idrisi evidence distinguished from contemporary observation. No doubtful exact camels/rice distribution generalized.

sources.title: Qazaqstan Tarihy, Kimek Khanate (ninth to early eleventh centuries)
sources.note: Original institutional history portal read. Used confederation, hereditary authority and neighboring relations. Excluded erroneous ninth-century Gardizi attribution, unqualified Yanmo identity and description of Manichaeism as Christian. Origin names critically compared with Tishin2018.

sources.title: V. V. Tishin, Kimak and Chu-mu-kun: Notes on an Identification (2018)
sources.note: Original Russian Academy of Sciences author abstract directly read, DOI10.17746/1563-0110.2018.46.3.107-113. Origin legend recorded by11th-century Gardizi; ethnic diversity and disputed equation Kimak/Yemak. No reconstructed Chinese etymology presented as settled fact.

sources.title: Helga Anetshofer, The Turkic Word qımız: Early Historical Textual Evidence and Origin (2023)
sources.note: Original scholarly paper, Zemin6:34-81, directly read and PDF saved. Printed37 and51-52: Gardizi c1050, qımız in external Persian source; printed52 Arabic-script form قمز visually verified in local render anetshofer-p52.png. No claim surviving autograph, universal Kimek alphabet, or exclusive invented beverage. Proposed distant etymology not adopted.

sources.title: G. N. Potanin Pavlodar Regional History Museum, Burial rite of the Kimek period in the Pavlodar Irtysh region (2021)
sources.note: Original museum archaeological account directly read in Russian. Mound groups, pottery with crushed-stone temper and neck impressions, animal bones interpreted feast remnants; fire steels/knives in male and female graves, horse equipment. Burial practice distinguished from ordinary meal sample or census of gendered work.

sources.title: I. V. Mertz, S. P. Grushin, S. A. Vasyutin, V. K. Mertz and V. L. Zheleznyakova, A Kimek burial at Semiyarka 2 (2025)
sources.note: Original article123-143 read via author full-text upload https://www.researchgate.net/publication/400020166_Kimakskoe_pogrebenie_na_poselenii_Semiarka_2_uznaa_cast_Srednego_Priirtysa; DOI direct fetch failed. Printed125-126 discovery and restoration,130-133 metal plaque details; dates second half9th-first half10th century, earlier than map. Early Iron Age settlement layer is separate from medieval burial. No health reconstruction from incomplete skeleton attempted.

sources.title: L. Turganbayeva, To the study of artistic metal of the Kimaks (2026)
sources.note: Original Margulan Institute researcher abstract directly read; Gumilyov Journal of History156(3):34-51, DOI10.32523/3080-129X-2026-156-3-34-51. Used reanalysis of excavated metalwork, geometric/floral motifs and Arslanova/Shulba context. Hypothesis of bird-shaman costume not generalized into proven medical practice.

sources.title: B. M. Khassenova, Gender in Kimek society according to archaeology, Steppe Panorama, issue4 (2019)
sources.note: Original journal abstract read in indexed text; direct access timed out. Issue explicitly2019, platform migrated2025. Finds differences in grave placement, food offerings and grave goods; Arslanova raised female status question from Upper Irtysh. No invented family household reconstruction or equality conclusion.

proposedOverrides.name: Kimek-Kipchak khaganate
proposedOverrides.summary: The Irtysh-centered confederation had earlier foundations, diverse communities and changing authority; its imported map window is 1000-1100.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One exact missing indexed ID; no aliases
batchIdentityNotes.interval: Imported1000-1100; earlier ninth/tenth-century formation and decline in eleventh century distinguished publicly.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: One world1000 polygon spans55.0607506-99.8703987E42.7922528-57.1980396N. Large eastward reach not asserted as precise sovereignty. Detailed archaeological examples focus on the Irtysh region; later western Cuman artifacts and Hungarian customs excluded.
batchIdentityNotes.overlap: Existing cuman-khanates and shared cuman-kipchak-confederation explicitly cover later western phases; Kimek was excluded from those identity associations. No separate modern nation taken as identical.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Secure externally transmitted Turkic qımız in Gardizi c1050, Arabic script as printed by modern scholar; not native autograph. Claims of inscriptions on regional mirrors exist but no deciphered exact specimen was verified for this card, so no guessed runiform letters supplied.
batchIdentityNotes.limits: No localized medical treatment, toilet installation or universal formal-school system securely established by checked sources. Craft skills, household mobility, seasonal food and social-role archaeology provide supported daily-life detail. Ethnonym origins remain debated.
